---
title: "Performance"
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

dir <- "performance"
startup <- read.csv(file.path(dir, "startup.csv"))
calls <- read.csv(file.path(dir, "calls.csv"))
versions <- read.csv(file.path(dir, "versions.csv"))

interfaces <- c("jlbind", "JuliaCall", "JuliaConnectoR")

# Format a time in seconds with a sensible unit.
fmt_time <- function(s) {
  ifelse(
    s < 1e-3,
    sprintf("%.3g µs", s * 1e6),
    ifelse(s < 1, sprintf("%.3g ms", s * 1e3), sprintf("%.3g s", s))
  )
}

# The results table of every section: a column per interface with the median
# time and, except for jlbind, how many times jlbind's median it is. `times` has
# a median per interface, `row_labels` optionally a named column of row labels.
results_table <- function(times, row_labels = NULL) {
  cells <- lapply(setNames(interfaces, interfaces), function(i) {
    ratio <- times[[i]] / times[["jlbind"]]
    ratio <- ifelse(
      ratio < 10,
      sprintf("%.1f×", ratio),
      sprintf("%.0f×", ratio)
    )
    if (i == "jlbind") {
      fmt_time(times[[i]])
    } else {
      sprintf("%s (%s)", fmt_time(times[[i]]), ratio)
    }
  })
  knitr::kable(
    as.data.frame(c(row_labels, cells), check.names = FALSE),
    align = "r",
    row.names = FALSE
  )
}

startup_med <- tapply(startup$seconds, startup$interface, median)[interfaces]
greet <- calls[calls$task == "greet", ]
greet_med <- setNames(greet$median, greet$interface)[interfaces]
shift <- calls[calls$task == "shift", ]
```

jlbind calls Julia code that was compiled ahead of time, through one
`.External()` per function. The alternatives,
[JuliaCall](https://github.com/JuliaInterop/JuliaCall) and
[JuliaConnectoR](https://github.com/stefan-m-lenz/JuliaConnectoR), run Julia
itself: JuliaCall embeds a Julia session in the R process, and JuliaConnectoR
starts one in a separate process and talks to it over a socket. This article
compares the three on the same Julia functions.

In short, on this machine, jlbind is ready to use
`r round(startup_med[["JuliaConnectoR"]] / startup_med[["jlbind"]])` to
`r round(startup_med[["JuliaCall"]] / startup_med[["jlbind"]])` times sooner,
and a call costs `r fmt_time(greet_med[["jlbind"]])` rather than
`r fmt_time(greet_med[["JuliaCall"]])` (JuliaCall) or
`r fmt_time(greet_med[["JuliaConnectoR"]])` (JuliaConnectoR).

## The benchmarks

The functions are those of `benchjl`, a minimal jlbind client kept next to the
benchmark script:

```julia
greet(name::String) = "Hello, " * name * "!"
shift(x::Vector{Float64}, by::Float64) = x .+ by
```

jlbind calls them through `benchjl`, compiled into a jlbind library. JuliaCall
and JuliaConnectoR evaluate the same definitions and call them with
`julia_call()` and `juliaFun()`. Each interface runs in fresh R processes, since
jlbind and JuliaCall can't share one.

- **Startup**: the median time from loading the package to the result of the
  first call, `greet("world")`, in a new R process (R's own startup excluded),
  over `r max(startup$rep)` repetitions.
- **Call overhead**: the median time of `greet("world")`, a string in and a
  string out, after the first call.
- **Data transfer**: the median time of `shift(x, 1)` for numeric vectors `x` of
  length 10 to 10^7^, which copies `x` to Julia and the result back.

Each table shows the median time for each interface and, in parentheses, how
many times jlbind's median it is.

The benchmark script is
[`vignettes/articles/performance/benchmark.R`](https://github.com/BjarkeHautop/jlbind/blob/main/vignettes/articles/performance/benchmark.R).
The results below were run on[^juliacall]:

```{r}
#| label: versions
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(versions, col.names = c("", ""))
```

[^juliacall]: Using the development version of JuliaCall, which fixes several
    issues, including failing on Ubuntu 24
    ([JuliaCall#265](https://github.com/JuliaInterop/JuliaCall/pull/265)).

## Startup

```{r}
#| label: startup-table
#| echo: false

results_table(startup_med)
```

For jlbind, startup is loading the compiled library and binding the package's
routines. JuliaCall and JuliaConnectoR start Julia, and compile each function
the first time it is called. With a real Julia package instead of two one-line
functions, the gap is usually larger: although Julia caches a package's
precompiled code across sessions, each new session still loads it and compiles
whatever the cache doesn't cover.

## Call overhead

```{r}
#| label: call-table
#| echo: false

results_table(greet_med)
```

A jlbind call is an `.External()` call into jlbind's C code, which calls the
compiled library directly, where the arguments are converted with R's C API.
JuliaCall converts arguments and looks up the function at run time in the
embedded session. JuliaConnectoR serializes the call to a separate Julia process
and the result back, so each call costs a round trip.

## Data transfer

```{r}
#| label: transfer-table
#| echo: false

wide <- reshape(
  shift[c("interface", "n", "median")],
  idvar = "n",
  timevar = "interface",
  direction = "wide"
)
names(wide) <- sub("median.", "", names(wide), fixed = TRUE)
results_table(
  wide,
  row_labels = list(
    Length = format(wide$n, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
  )
)
```
